answer.rationale: Constraints eliminate most directions before memory even matters: rollback_release is ruled out by compliance (memory_b1 is moot here regardless of how good it looked on day 18); regional_failover (memory_b2) during a settlement write peak risks in-flight write loss, which directly violates the 'without losing customer writes' objective; enable_circuit_breaker (memory_b4) works by failing fast, which sheds writes — wrong tool for a write-path saturation at peak; add_capacity (memory_b3) succeeded only because it was provisioned BEFORE the peak, and provisioning latency means it likely will not relieve a 90-minute-old climb mid-peak. That leaves route_read_replicas, which is the only option that reduces contention on the primary without discarding writes, and is cheaply reversible. I am spending the single verification on memory_b5 because it is the memory I am actually leaning on, and its record is the one most likely to be context-mismatched: 'report queries / dashboard load' is a very different read profile than settlement-peak read pressure, and I need the original record to see whether the primary was write-saturated or merely read-contended, and what fraction of load actually moved. Uncertainty I am not resolving: none of these memories establishes the CAUSE of the current climb. The release two hours ago is the obvious suspect by timing, and since we cannot revert it, replica routing may only buy headroom rather than fix anything — it could mask a regression that keeps worsening. Also note the inherited memory is uniformly success stories with no recorded failures or costs; that one-sidedness is a survivorship artifact of how this archive was consolidated, so I am treating each entry as weaker evidence than its confident tone suggests rather than as a validated playbook. Staged ramp: route a bounded slice of read traffic first, watch replica lag and write p99 together, and hold the rest pending evidence — replica lag under heavy writes is the specific way this action can backfire and serve stale data, so it must not go out as a single broad flip.
